title: Copy List with Random Pointer
directAnswer: Deep-copy a list whose nodes each have a next and an arbitrary random pointer. The clean answer maps each original node to its clone in a hash map, then wires up next and random on the clones by looking them up. O(n) time, O(n) space. The follow-up O(1)-space trick interleaves each clone right after its original, sets random from the neighbour, then unzips the two lists.

rules: Map **original node → clone node**; the random pointers force you to resolve nodes you may not have created yet, so build all clones first.
Use `map.get(...)` / `dict.get(...)` so a **null** next or random maps to null, not a crash.
Two passes: pass 1 creates every clone, pass 2 wires next and random. One pass can't work because random can point forward.
For O(1) space, **interleave** clone after original (A→A'→B→B'…), set `clone.random = orig.random.next`, then carefully **unzip**.
When unzipping, restore the original list's next pointers too — leaving them interleaved is a silent corruption bug.
whenToUse: Deep-copy any structure with arbitrary cross-references, not just sequential next pointers
Cloning a graph-like object where you must map originals to copies (Clone Graph is the same idea)
Any time you must resolve references to nodes that may not be constructed yet
Serializing/duplicating linked structures with back- or forward-pointers
antiSignals: There is no random/cross pointer → a plain single-pass copy suffices
You're allowed to share nodes (shallow copy) → no mapping needed
The structure is acyclic and only points backward → you could resolve on the fly without a map
remember.takeaway: An old→new hash map is the universal deep-copy tool for structures with arbitrary pointers — the exact same trick clones graphs. The interleaving method is a neat O(1)-space flex, but the map version is the one to lead with for clarity.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you handle arbitrary (possibly forward) references by separating 'create all nodes' from 'wire up pointers', and whether you null-safely resolve next/random.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to set random in a single pass and dereferencing a clone that doesn't exist yet, or crashing on null random/next instead of mapping null to null.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Lead with the clean two-pass hash map, then offer the O(1)-space interleave-and-split as the follow-up, and stress restoring the original list when unzipping.

problemStatement:
A linked list of length n is given such that each node contains an additional random pointer, which could point to any node in the list, or `null`.

Construct a **deep copy** of the list. The deep copy should consist of exactly n brand-new nodes, where each new node's value is set to the value of its corresponding original node. Both the next and random pointers of the new nodes should point to new nodes in the copied list such that the pointers in the original and copied list represent the same list state. None of the pointers in the new list should point to nodes in the original list.

Return the head of the copied linked list.
constraints: Node.random is null or points to some node in the list
The new list must be completely independent of the original
understanding: We must produce a brand-new list of n nodes whose next and random pointers mirror the original's structure but reference only the new nodes. The challenge is the random pointer: it can point anywhere, including to a node we haven't cloned yet, so we can't just copy as we walk.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the random pointer point to any node, including itself or null?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — it can target any node in the list, the node itself, or be null. That's why I resolve it through a map rather than computing an offset.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the copy be fully independent of the original?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Completely. No pointer in the new list may reference an original node, and the original must be left intact.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is O(n) extra space acceptable, or do you want O(1)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll present the clean O(n) hash-map solution first; if you want the follow-up, the interleave-and-split method achieves O(1) auxiliary space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return for an empty list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return null. Both approaches guard the empty case naturally.

examples.explanation: Each pair is [val, random_index]. The clone reproduces values, next order, and random targets using only new nodes.
Both nodes' random point to index 1 (the second node); the copy mirrors that with its own nodes.
Empty input copies to an empty list — return null.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The hash-map two-pass is the clear default; interleave-and-split is the O(1)-space follow-up flex.

approaches.name: Hash Map — Old Node → New Node (Optimal for Clarity)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. It's the cleanest, hardest-to-get-wrong answer and the one most interviewers expect first.
hints: The random pointer can point to a node you haven't copied yet. What if you created every clone first, before touching any pointers?
Pass 1: walk the list and for each original node make a bare clone (just the value), storing original → clone in a hash map.
Pass 2: walk again and for each original set clone.next = map[original.next] and clone.random = map[original.random], using a null-safe lookup so null maps to null.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two linear passes (create, then wire) → O(n) time. The map holds one entry per node → O(n) space, plus the n new nodes themselves.
approaches.explanation:
We sidestep the forward-reference problem by building all the nodes first and wiring their pointers second.

**Why one pass fails.** If you tried to set `clone.random` while creating clones left to right, `original.random` might point to a node further along that you haven't cloned yet — so there's no clone to point at. The fix is to decouple *existence* from *linkage*.

**Pass 1 — create every clone.** Walk the original list and, for each node, allocate a new node carrying the same `val`. Record the correspondence in a hash map: `map[original] = clone`. After this pass, every original node has a clone, regardless of where any random pointer leads.

**Pass 2 — wire next and random.** Walk the original list again. For each `original`, set `map[original].next = map[original.next]` and `map[original].random = map[original.random]`. Because all clones already exist, every lookup succeeds. Critically, use a *null-safe* lookup (`map.get(...)` returning null for a missing/null key) so that a null `next` or `random` becomes null in the clone instead of throwing.

**Why it's fully independent.** Every pointer in the new list is the *result of a map lookup*, so it always resolves to a clone — never to an original node. The original list is read but never mutated.
approaches.insight: The map converts 'I need the clone of an arbitrary original node' into an O(1) lookup, which is exactly what arbitrary cross-references demand. This is the identical strategy used to clone a general graph — the random pointer is just one extra edge per node.

pitfalls: Indexing the map directly on a null key (map.get(null) is safe, but map[null] in some languages is not).
Trying to set random during a single creation pass — the target clone may not exist yet.
Returning the original head instead of oldToNew.get(head).

approaches.name: Interleave & Split — O(1) Extra Space
approaches.whenToMention: Bring this out for the explicit 'can you do it without the hash map?' follow-up. Warn that the unzip step is bug-prone.
hints: Instead of a map to find each clone, what if each clone lived right next to its original so you could reach it via original.next?
Pass 1: insert each clone immediately after its original (A → A' → B → B' → ...). Pass 2: set clone.random = original.random.next, since original.random.next IS the clone of original.random.
Pass 3: unzip the interleaved list back into two — restore the originals' next pointers AND extract the clones' next pointers.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Three linear passes (interleave, set random, unzip) → O(n) time. No hash map; only a few pointers are used → O(1) auxiliary space (the n new nodes are required output, not counted).
approaches.explanation:
We eliminate the map by physically placing each clone next to its original, so 'the clone of X' is simply `X.next`.

**Pass 1 — interleave.** For each original node, create its clone and splice it directly after: `clone.next = orig.next; orig.next = clone`. The list becomes A → A' → B → B' → C → C'. Now every clone is reachable from its original in one hop.

**Pass 2 — assign random pointers.** For each original `orig` (stepping two at a time), the clone is `orig.next`. The clone's random should be the clone of `orig.random`, which — thanks to interleaving — is exactly `orig.random.next`. So `orig.next.random = orig.random.next` (guarding for `orig.random == null`). This is the elegant core: the map lookup became a `.next`.

**Pass 3 — unzip.** Now separate the two interleaved lists. Walk through and, for each original, set `orig.next = orig.next.next` (skip the clone) and `clone.next = clone.next.next` (skip the next original) — being careful not to dereference null at the tail. This both extracts the clone list AND **restores the original list** to its initial state, which is required: leaving the lists interleaved silently corrupts the input.

**Why it's correct and independent.** Every clone pointer is derived from a clone (`*.next` of an original gives a clone), so no clone references an original after the unzip. The price is the fiddly three-pass pointer surgery — powerful for the space win, but easy to botch under pressure.
approaches.insight: Interleaving turns the hash map into adjacency: 'clone of X' becomes 'X.next'. It's a beautiful O(1)-space trick, but the unzip must restore the original list too — forgetting that is the most common way candidates get it marked wrong.

dryRun.intro: Interleave, then set random from neighbours, then split.

code.python:
def copyRandomList(self, head: 'Node') -> 'Node':
    if not head:
        return None

    # Pass 1: interleave clones after originals
    cur = head
    while cur:
        clone = Node(cur.val)
        clone.next = cur.next
        cur.next = clone
        cur = clone.next

    # Pass 2: assign random pointers on the clones
    cur = head
    while cur:
        cur.next.random = cur.random.next if cur.random else None
        cur = cur.next.next

    # Pass 3: unzip the two lists
    dummy = Node(0)
    copy_tail = dummy
    cur = head
    while cur:
        clone = cur.next
        cur.next = clone.next      # restore original
        copy_tail.next = clone     # build copy
        copy_tail = clone
        cur = cur.next
    return dummy.next

java.explanation: Splice clone in right after its original so clone == original.next.
The clone of cur.random is cur.random.next — the interleaving makes this hold; guard for null.
Unzip: restore the ORIGINAL list's next pointer (mandatory — don't leave it interleaved).
Extract the clone into the independent copy list.

pitfalls: Forgetting to restore the original list's next in the unzip — corrupts the input.
Dereferencing cur.random.next without the null check on cur.random.
Mismatching the two-step advance and walking off the end of the interleaved list.

commonMistakes: Setting random in a single pass before all clones exist — the target may be uncreated.
Crashing on a null next or random instead of mapping null to null.
In the interleave method, failing to restore the original list during the unzip.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Resolving random before the clone exists
commonMistakesDetailed.why: random can point forward. If you create and fully wire a node in one pass, original.random may have no clone yet, giving null or a crash.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
cur = head
while cur:
    clone = Node(cur.val)
    clone.random = old_to_new.get(cur.random)  # cur.random not cloned yet!
    old_to_new[cur] = clone
    cur = cur.next
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
cur = head
while cur:                       # pass 1: create all clones
    old_to_new[cur] = Node(cur.val)
    cur = cur.next
cur = head
while cur:                       # pass 2: wire pointers
    old_to_new[cur].next = old_to_new.get(cur.next)
    old_to_new[cur].random = old_to_new.get(cur.random)
    cur = cur.next

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not restoring the original list when unzipping
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The interleave method mutates the input. If you only extract clones and leave originals pointing at clones, you've corrupted the caller's list.

patternNote: Old→new hash mapping for deep-copying structures with arbitrary references — the same approach clones graphs and trees-with-random-pointers. The interleave-and-split variant is the niche O(1)-space optimization to reach for only when memory is constrained.
